Hinged Napoleon

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three equal-sided triangles sit on the sides of a triangle, and their centres make another equal-sided one.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Slide Turn to spin the hinged pieces, choose which pair swivels, and tick Show names.
Look for the math

Move a corner of the big triangle and the small construction changes with it, yet the three centre dots still make an equal-sided triangle. The original cut-the-knot page still embeds its Java applet; this page redraws the same hinges with SVG. The page credits the proof it shows to Alex Anderson, who also published it in the journal Kvant.

Napoleon's triangle

On each side of ABC stand an equilateral triangle. Mark the centre of each one: Ac on BC, Bc on CA and Cc on AB. Napoleon's theorem says these three centres always form an equilateral triangle, whether the three triangles point outwards or all inwards. The logic test checks both choices over more than a hundred triangles, including flat and very wide ones: the three sides of AcBcCc agree to within a drawing-scale tolerance of 10-7.

What the hinges do

The applet's scrollbar is built with a maximum of 125 and a visible part of 5, so it can actually show the whole numbers 0…120. Its three radio boxes pick which pair turns: B, C (the starting choice) turns the pieces hinged at Bc and Cc; A, C and A, B turn the other pairs. Each turn is an ordinary rotation about a centre dot. The logic test transcribes the applet's own Compute() a second time and compares every point of all five translucent pieces for all 121 × 3 settings on dozens of triangles; they agree.

With no corner wider than 120°, the page's angle sums hold: ∠A'BC' = ∠ABC + 60°, ∠A'CB' = ∠ACB + 60° and ∠B'AC' = ∠BAC + 60°. Setting the turn to 120° makes B and C land on A (or A and C on B, or A and B on C), because the relevant small triangles are isosceles with a 120° apex. Then the three angles add to 180° + 3 × 60° = 360°, so the hinged sides close into one segment AA*.

Why the middle triangle is equal-sided

When the pieces close, AcBcCc is cut into three triangles congruent to ABcCc, AcBCc and AcBcC. The logic test adds their areas and compares with the area of AcBcCc for every triangle with no angle over 120°: the difference is at most a rounding error. Side-side-side then makes the assembled triangle match AcBcCc; the three angles at its corners are each 60°, so it is equiangular and therefore equilateral.

There is another way to see the same point. Reflect A in the line BcCc, B in AcCc and C in AcBc: the three images coincide, and the common point sees the corners at 120° each. It lies on the three circumcircles of the outer equilateral triangles, which is the Fermat point of ABC. The test checks the coincident images and the three 120° angles on every such triangle.

The page's proviso

The page says its proof assumes no angle of ABC exceeds 120° and must be changed otherwise. That warning is correct. Dragging C close to AB can make an angle of about 172°: the centre triangle is still equilateral and the hinges still close, but the three hinge angles now add to about 255°, not 360°, and the reflected point sees angles of 120°, 60° and 60°, so it is no longer the Fermat point. The page's dissection argument only covers triangles with all angles below 120°; Napoleon's theorem itself covers every triangle. This port keeps the applet's rules and ranges; the AWT scrollbar, checkboxes and serif labels became a slider, buttons and site-coloured SVG, and a Reset button was added for convenience.

Try B, C at 120° and watch the two green corners meet on A; then drag one corner until its angle passes 120° and read what the status says.
